title: Our Planetary System
intro: Compare the Sun, planets, and small bodies as parts of one system. Use their shared patterns, distinct planet families, and spacecraft observations to reason about how the system works.

sections.title: A map of the solar system

img.alt: The Sun, inner planets, asteroid belt, outer planets, Kuiper belt, and distant small bodies arranged outward by orbital region.

steps.title: Regions and scale
bullets: The Sun dominates the system's mass and supplies most of its energy. The planets orbit at distances that grow dramatically from the inner rocky worlds to the outer giants.
The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter. Beyond Neptune, the Kuiper belt contains many icy bodies, including dwarf planets.
A diagram that enlarges planets for visibility cannot also show their actual distances to the same scale; apparent spacing in such a drawing is not a measurement.

steps.title: The solar system includes more than planets
bullets: The solar system includes the Sun and every body gravitationally bound to it: planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids, comets, and smaller debris.
A body's orbit and physical properties help astronomers classify it; being round or large alone does not make an object one of the eight major planets.

boxes.text: Knowing where a body formed and where it orbits helps explain its composition, temperature, and interactions with the rest of the system.
Move outward from the Sun: rocky planets, asteroid belt, giant planets, then distant icy populations.
A not-to-scale solar-system picture is useful for identifying order and categories, but it cannot be used to compare both planet sizes and orbital distances.

sourceNotes: The Cosmic Perspective, 10th ed., Chapter 7, sections 7.1-7.2.

sections.title: Terrestrial and jovian worlds

img.alt: A side-by-side comparison of terrestrial rocky planets and larger, gas-rich jovian planets.

steps.title: Two useful comparisons
bullets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are the terrestrial planets: relatively small, rocky, and dense, with solid surfaces.
Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune are the jovian planets: much larger, with thick envelopes rich in hydrogen compounds and extensive moon systems.
Jovian planets are not all identical. Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, while Uranus and Neptune contain larger proportions of substances that astronomers classify as ices.

steps.title: Compare properties, not just names
bullets: Planetary families differ in size, composition, average density, atmosphere, and moons. A single property does not explain every contrast.
Comparing planets with similar properties can reveal meaningful exceptions, such as a world with an unusually thick atmosphere or a strongly tilted rotation axis.

boxes.text: Comparative planetology uses similarities and differences to test how planets formed and how their environments changed.
Terrestrial means rocky inner planets; jovian means the larger outer planets and their distinct giant-planet properties.
Do not infer that every jovian planet has the same composition or structure; Uranus and Neptune differ from Jupiter and Saturn.

sections.title: The four terrestrial planets

steps.title: Mercury and Venus
bullets: Mercury has almost no substantial atmosphere, so its surface experiences large temperature contrasts and preserves abundant impact craters.
Venus is similar to Earth in size but has a dense carbon-dioxide atmosphere and an extreme greenhouse effect. Similar size does not imply similar surface conditions.
The slowly rotating or backward-rotating inner planets show that planetary spin directions are not all identical.

img.alt: The inner terrestrial planets are grouped separately from the outer giants.

steps.title: Earth and Mars
bullets: Earth's liquid-water surface, atmosphere, and active geology make it a distinctive habitable world, not a representative sample of every planet.
Mars is cold and dry at the surface today, but its channels, minerals, and other evidence indicate that liquid water flowed there in the past.
A planet's present conditions can differ greatly from its earlier history; surface features and rocks preserve clues to change.

boxes.text: The inner planets formed in the warmer part of the solar nebula, where rock and metal could condense but water ice could not remain stable as readily.
Earth and Venus are similar in size, yet their surface environments are dramatically different.
Evidence for ancient water on Mars does not mean liquid water is stable across most of its surface today.

sourceNotes: The Cosmic Perspective, 10th ed., Chapter 7, planetary profiles and sections 7.1-7.2.

sections.title: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune

steps.title: Giant planets are systems of their own
bullets: Jupiter and Saturn are massive hydrogen-rich gas giants with deep atmospheres, rings, and many moons.
Uranus and Neptune are also giant planets, but their composition includes a larger fraction of water, ammonia, and methane than Jupiter's and Saturn's.
A giant planet's moons can have active geology, subsurface oceans, atmospheres, or other environments unlike the planet itself.

img.alt: Jovian planets are compared, including gas giants and ice giants.

steps.title: Distinctive rotations and rings
bullets: Saturn's rings are broad but extremely thin relative to their diameter, and are made of countless pieces of ice and rock.
Uranus rotates with an extreme axial tilt, making its seasonal illumination unusual.
The presence of rings or many moons is characteristic of the giant-planet systems, but those features do not mean the planets are solid all the way through.

boxes.text: A planet and its moons form a linked system: gravity, tidal heating, impacts, and sunlight can shape each moon differently.
Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.
A ring system is not a solid disk. It consists of many separate orbiting particles.

sections.title: Asteroids, comets, and dwarf planets

img.alt: The asteroid belt is shown between the inner rocky planets and the outer giants, with distant icy bodies beyond Neptune.

steps.title: Small bodies occupy distinct regions
bullets: Asteroids are rocky or metallic bodies. Many orbit in the belt between Mars and Jupiter, though asteroid orbits occur elsewhere too.
Comets contain substantial ice mixed with dust and rock. When a comet approaches the Sun, heating releases gas and dust that form a coma and tails.
The Kuiper belt beyond Neptune contains icy bodies, including Pluto. The more distant Oort cloud is inferred to be a reservoir for many long-period comets.

steps.title: A coma and tail are temporary
bullets: A comet's tail forms as solar heating releases material, while sunlight and the solar wind push that material away from the Sun.
A comet can travel through most of its orbit without a conspicuous tail. The bright display develops mainly near the Sun.

steps.title: Planets and dwarf planets
bullets: Dwarf planets orbit the Sun and are massive enough to become nearly round, but they have not cleared their orbital neighborhoods of other sizable bodies.
Pluto's classification reflects a formal category based on orbital-neighborhood clearing, not a claim that Pluto is uninteresting or geologically inactive.

boxes.text: The distribution of icy and rocky small bodies preserves clues about the temperatures and mixing of material in the early solar system.
A comet's tail points generally away from the Sun, not necessarily behind the comet along its direction of travel.
The asteroid belt is not a crowded ring of planet-sized objects; its members are separated by large distances.

sourceNotes: The Cosmic Perspective, 10th ed., Chapter 7, sections 7.1-7.2.

sections.title: Patterns that reveal the system's history

steps.title: A shared direction and plane
bullets: Most planets orbit the Sun in the same direction and in nearly the same plane. Most also rotate in the same general direction as their orbits.
These coordinated motions are evidence that the solar system formed from a rotating, flattened cloud rather than from unrelated objects captured at random.
Exceptions such as unusual rotation directions and highly tilted axes are important evidence, not reasons to discard the overall pattern.

img.alt: A collapsing cloud forms a rotating disk in which planetesimals accumulate.

steps.title: The nebular hypothesis
bullets: The nebular hypothesis describes the solar system forming as gravity collapsed a cloud of gas and dust, producing a young Sun surrounded by a rotating disk.
Material in the disk collided and accumulated into planetesimals, which grew into planets and smaller bodies.
The temperature gradient in the disk helps explain why rocky material dominated near the Sun while ices could also accumulate farther out.

steps.title: Test a model with multiple observations
bullets: A successful formation model must explain common orbital patterns, the differences between inner and outer planets, and the existence of smaller-body reservoirs.
A model should also account for exceptions and make predictions that can be compared with observations of other planetary systems.

boxes.text: A rotating disk naturally produces a flattened system with many bodies orbiting in a shared direction.
Observation first: identify a pattern. Explanation next: decide what formation process could produce it.
The nebular hypothesis is not supported by one similarity alone; it must explain many independent patterns and survive tests.

sourceNotes: The Cosmic Perspective, 10th ed., Chapter 7, section 7.2.

sections.title: How spacecraft explore other worlds

img.alt: Flyby, orbital, lander, and rover mission paths around and on a planetary body.

steps.title: Match the mission to the question
bullets: A flyby passes a target and can survey many objects, but its close observation window is brief.
An orbiter circles a world for repeated measurements and broad mapping, but reaching and maintaining orbit requires additional energy and propulsion.
A lander or rover can make direct surface measurements. Its observations are detailed but limited to a small region and depend on landing safely.

steps.title: Remote sensing and direct measurements
bullets: Cameras and spectrometers remotely measure reflected or emitted light; radar can reveal surfaces through some clouds and darkness.
Landers and rovers examine local conditions, while sample-return missions can bring material to laboratories on Earth.
Mission design balances scientific goals, communication delay, power, travel time, hazards, and cost.

boxes.text: No single mission type answers every question. Remote coverage, repeated orbital views, and local sampling provide different kinds of evidence.
Flyby: brief pass. Orbiter: repeated global views. Lander or rover: local surface evidence.
A photograph alone does not replace compositional measurements or direct surface analysis; each method has different limits.

cards.back: A relatively small, rocky, dense planet of the inner solar system.
A large outer planet with a deep atmosphere and an extensive moon system.
Jupiter or Saturn, a giant planet dominated by hydrogen and helium.
Uranus or Neptune, giant planets with a larger fraction of water, ammonia, and methane than Jupiter or Saturn.
A small rocky or metallic body orbiting the Sun.
An ice-rich small body that can release gas and dust when heated near the Sun.
cards.short: Icy body that can grow a coma and tail.

cards.back: A region beyond Neptune containing many icy bodies, including dwarf planets.
A distant, roughly spherical reservoir inferred to supply many long-period comets.
A Sun-orbiting body massive enough to be nearly round but not to have cleared its orbital neighborhood.
cards.short: Round body that has not cleared its orbit.

cards.back: The model that the solar system formed from a collapsing, rotating cloud of gas and dust that flattened into a disk.
cards.short: A rotating disk formed from a collapsing cloud.

cards.back: A spacecraft mission that passes a target without entering orbit or landing.
cards.short: Brief close pass of a target.

cards.back: A spacecraft that remains in orbit to make repeated observations of a world.
A spacecraft designed to reach a body's surface and make measurements at a fixed location.
The study of worlds by comparing their similarities and differences to test explanations for their histories and processes.
cards.short: Use differences and similarities to test planetary explanations.

quiz.q: A diagram enlarges all planets but preserves their order from the Sun. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The planet order is shown, but the drawn sizes or gaps may not represent actual scale.
The gaps between every neighboring orbit are equal.
The sizes and distances are both accurately represented.
The asteroid belt must be denser than the rings of Saturn.
quiz.why: A schematic can preserve the order of bodies while changing sizes or distances so the objects can be seen.

quiz.q: Which observation best supports classifying Earth with the terrestrial planets rather than with the jovian planets?
options: It is a comparatively small, dense world with a rocky surface.
It has a moon that orbits it.
It travels around the Sun.
It reflects sunlight into space.
quiz.why: Rocky composition, small size, and higher density are characteristic of the terrestrial family.

quiz.q: A student groups Uranus with Jupiter because both are enormous compared with Earth. What important distinction should be added?
options: Uranus is an ice giant, while Jupiter is a gas giant.
Uranus is a terrestrial planet, while Jupiter is a dwarf planet.
Uranus orbits beyond the Kuiper belt, while Jupiter is inside the asteroid belt.
Uranus has no atmosphere, while Jupiter has one.
quiz.why: Both are giant planets, but Uranus and Neptune have a different composition from hydrogen-rich Jupiter and Saturn.

quiz.q: Two planets have similar radii, but one has a dense carbon-dioxide atmosphere and a far hotter surface. Which inference is strongest?
options: Similar size alone does not determine a planet's surface environment.
Their surface conditions must be identical because their sizes are similar.
The denser atmosphere proves the hotter planet formed farther from the Sun.
The hotter planet cannot be terrestrial.
quiz.why: Venus and Earth illustrate that comparable size does not guarantee similar atmospheric or surface conditions.

quiz.q: A cratered world has almost no atmosphere to redistribute heat. Which additional observation would best fit Mercury?
options: Large temperature contrasts between its day and night sides.
Clouds that hide nearly all surface features.
A global ocean beneath a thick atmosphere.
A tail that always points along its orbit.
quiz.why: With little atmosphere, Mercury cannot efficiently redistribute heat around the planet.

quiz.q: Which evidence most directly supports the claim that Mars had flowing liquid water in its past?
options: Surface channels and minerals associated with water-altered environments.
Its current surface temperature is always above water's boiling point.
Its two small moons are made of ice.
Its orbit is nearly circular.
quiz.why: Surface landforms and altered minerals preserve evidence for ancient water even though surface liquid water is not broadly stable today.

quiz.q: A probe detects many narrow ring features around a giant planet. What is the best physical interpretation?
options: The rings consist of many separate particles orbiting the planet.
The rings are a single rigid sheet attached to the planet.
The rings are the planet's solid surface viewed edge-on.
The rings are trails left by planets that escaped the system.
quiz.why: Planetary rings are made from large numbers of separate pieces of ice and rock.

quiz.q: A body is round and orbits the Sun, but many sizable objects share its orbital region. Which classification best fits?
options: Dwarf planet
Major planet
Moon
Cometary tail
quiz.why: A dwarf planet can be round and orbit the Sun without clearing its orbital neighborhood.

quiz.q: Why can a comet become much more visible as it approaches the Sun?
options: Heating releases gas and dust that create a coma and tails.
Its orbital speed converts its whole body into visible light.
The Sun pulls it into a permanent ring.
Its surface turns into a liquid ocean.
quiz.why: Solar heating causes volatile material to escape from an icy comet, producing a coma and tails.

quiz.q: A comet's tail points away from the Sun even while the comet is moving toward the Sun. What does this show?
options: Tail direction is not simply the direction opposite to the comet's motion.
The comet must be orbiting backward.
The comet's tail is a solid extension of its nucleus.
All comet tails point behind the comet's orbital path.
quiz.why: Sunlight and the solar wind push tail material away from the Sun, so the tail need not trail the comet's motion.

quiz.q: Which pairing of small-body population and location is most accurate?
options: Kuiper belt — beyond Neptune
Asteroid belt — beyond the Oort cloud
Oort cloud — between Earth and Mars
Kuiper belt — inside Mercury's orbit
quiz.why: The Kuiper belt is a population of icy objects beyond Neptune.

quiz.q: A long-period comet approaches the inner solar system from a highly extended orbit. Which distant source is most strongly associated with such comets?
options: The Oort cloud
The asteroid belt
Saturn's rings
The terrestrial planets
quiz.why: The distant, roughly spherical Oort cloud is inferred to supply many long-period comets.

quiz.q: Which pattern is most consistent with planets forming in a rotating disk?
options: Most planets orbit in nearly the same plane and direction.
Every planet has the same orbital period.
All moons orbit in exactly the same plane as their planet.
Every planet rotates at the same rate.
quiz.why: A rotating, flattened disk naturally produces coordinated orbital directions and a shared orbital plane.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly describes the nebular hypothesis?
options: A rotating cloud of gas and dust collapsed and flattened into a disk from which the Sun and planets formed.
The planets formed independently and were later captured into random orbits by the Sun.
The Sun formed first as a solid object and later split into the planets.
Comets collided to create the gas cloud that became the Sun.
quiz.why: The model begins with a collapsing, rotating cloud that forms a central Sun and a surrounding disk.

quiz.q: Why does the nebular model predict rocky planets closer to the Sun and icy material farther out?
options: The early disk had a temperature gradient that affected which materials could condense.
The Sun's gravity only affected rocky material near its surface.
Icy objects cannot orbit inside the asteroid belt today.
The outer planets formed before the Sun began to shine.
quiz.why: Temperature varied across the disk, so different materials could condense in different regions.

quiz.q: A model explains the shared orbital plane but cannot explain why the inner planets are rocky and the outer planets are giant worlds. What is the best scientific response?
options: Treat the model as incomplete and test a mechanism that explains both patterns.
Ignore the compositional evidence because one pattern already fits.
Change the observations until they match the model.
Conclude that all planets formed independently.
quiz.why: A useful formation model must account for multiple independent patterns, not just one.

quiz.q: A spacecraft must map a planet repeatedly over several years. Which mission design best fits that goal?
options: Orbiter
Flyby
Atmospheric entry probe with no transmitter
One-time impactor
quiz.why: An orbiter can make repeated measurements and survey a world from many viewing angles.

quiz.q: A mission needs high-resolution measurements of soil chemistry at one safe landing site. Which approach is most direct?
options: Lander or rover
Distant flyby only
Telescope on Earth
A second planet's moon
quiz.why: A lander or rover can directly analyze the local surface, although it samples only a limited area.

quiz.q: Why might scientists choose a flyby instead of an orbiter for a mission to several small bodies?
options: A flyby can visit multiple targets without carrying the fuel needed to orbit each one.
A flyby provides continuous global mapping of each target for years.
A flyby can collect surface samples without approaching a target.
A flyby removes communication delays.
quiz.why: Flybys trade long-duration coverage for the ability to encounter multiple targets with a simpler trajectory.

quiz.q: A thick atmosphere prevents a camera from seeing the surface clearly. Which method could provide complementary surface information?
options: Radar remote sensing or measurements from a probe that enters the atmosphere.
A visible-light image from a farther distance.
A measurement of the planet's orbital direction only.
A telescope pointed at the planet's rings.
quiz.why: Radar can penetrate some cloud layers, and atmospheric probes can make measurements below the clouds.

quiz.q: What is a key limitation of a rover compared with an orbiter?
options: It makes detailed measurements over a very limited surface area.
It cannot send any scientific data.
It observes only the planet's global magnetic field.
It must remain outside the atmosphere.
quiz.why: Surface missions provide local detail but cannot directly survey the entire planet.

quiz.q: A scientist compares the number of moons, surface geology, and atmospheric composition across several planets. What is the central purpose of this comparison?
options: To use similarities and differences to test explanations of planetary history.
To determine that planets with moons must be more massive than the Sun.
To prove that every world formed in a separate system.
To replace measurements with visual resemblance.
quiz.why: Comparative planetology tests hypotheses by examining patterns and exceptions among worlds.

quiz.q: A spacecraft returns a rock sample, while an orbiter maps the full planet. Why are both missions scientifically useful?
options: The sample gives detailed local composition while orbital data supplies broad context.
The sample determines the entire planet's surface history by itself.
Orbital mapping reveals no information about surface features.
The two data types measure the same thing at the same scale.
quiz.why: Local analysis and global mapping are complementary forms of evidence.

quiz.q: Which conclusion best combines the orbital and compositional patterns of the solar system?
options: A rotating, temperature-structured disk can explain both shared orbital motions and inner-to-outer composition differences.
The planets' common direction proves that all have identical compositions.
The locations of asteroids show that planets do not orbit the Sun.
The differences among planets rule out a common formation process.
quiz.why: The nebular model links the rotating disk's geometry with temperature-dependent material condensation.
